doc.title: Derek Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 5, 2021

title: Grad school burnout, Texas freedom, and influences Harris and McFerrin
summary: After comparison burnout in grad school he moved to Abilene Christian, worked on slap tongue freely, and was inspired by Eddie Harris and Bobby McFerrin.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: It must have grabbed your personal attention when you realized that you had the facility, you had like this super embouchure. Right?

Well okay. It probably didn’t happen overnight. But you realized in the practice room somewhere, okay I can slap tongue and now what’s the next step and you start adding these things on. And I’m trying to think of what my question is, but you’re talking about
would I listen to that and so when was the first time you tried that by yourself in front of an audience?

Oh yeah, yeah. Well a cool thing is that I was able to do it online first in the sense of posting a YouTube video. Yes I had experimented a little bit before. I was teaching down in Texas, Abeline Christian University, I was a full time instructor for six years. And that time was really good for me. So I did undergrad, Hope College; graduate school University of Cincinnati. And when you’re a student you’re learning so, so much. But there’s also this kind of underwritten kind of competition. There’s this intensity of kind of always comparing yourself. And I didn’t do so well with that. Like I think it was good for my growth and getting me to practice, because wow, they practice a lot, that’s what I’m going to do. But I almost kind of burnt out at that point. And that was when I didn’t know what I had to say, I didn’t know what kind of music I wanted to play. I was studying kind of more or less traditional jazz. But then it took me, moving down to Texas and being a professor. And I had income coming in, I had free time on my hands, and it was like oh yeah, I have this saxophone here. Am I going to practice? I should practice this. What do I want — and there was this freedom to like, if I’m going to play this thing I’m just going to play it exactly how I want to play. I’m not going to play it — I’m not going to do the things that other people want me to do, the things that a good jazz musician is supposed to do. Yeah sometimes I would do that stuff, because I wanted to be good at improvising. But it was like that slap tonguing thing that I remember hearing, I want to figure that out. That’s really cool to me. And so I don’t care if I take three hours just straight up working on slap tongue each day, I’m going to do it, because I can. And I know not everyone has that luxury. And I’m even grateful — I think if I had moved to like New York City right after grad school and into that scene, I don’t think I ever would have kind of come across this solo type of playing. Because I would have just been hustling trying to get every gig, every group I could do, I’d be doing wedding bands, bar mitzvahs, all that. And that’s good stuff. And some people, and I don’t want to knock that stuff because some people do that stuff, they love it, they thrive with it and they still have time on their own to do that. But for me it was really good just kind of taking it a little bit slower after I had already worked on these skills of improvising and good tone in college. And now what do I want to do. If I’m really honest, what do I want to work on. Because I don’t have to play this music. And that was kind of freeing for me. I don’t have to play it. And so if I’m going to play it I’m going to play it how I want to. And just slowly I realized I like this percussive stuff. And some of the people I was listening to like the Eddie Harris’s with the jumping around of the octaves, and then the big one for me, Bobby McFerrin, of course not a sax player, a vocalist.
